text:
A lake has far fewer fish than its size would lead us to expect. At first scientists thought there was too little food, but surveys have since found plenty of insects and plankton for fish to eat. A more likely cause is a lack of oxygen. A power station on the shore releases warm water into the lake, and warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water. Parts of the lake further from the power station would receive less of this warm water.
Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen this explanation?
options: Fish become more numerous the further one goes from the power station's outflow.
Some species of fish need very little oxygen.
Fish were introduced to the lake only twenty years ago.
Other lakes beside power stations have plenty of fish.
The insects in the lake are eaten mainly by birds.
solution: The explanation predicts that oxygen, and so fish, should increase away from the warm outflow. Finding exactly that pattern supports it. Other lakes with power stations and plenty of fish count against it; fish that need little oxygen and the late introduction of fish do not test the explanation; birds eating insects revives the food explanation.

text:
Mia needs 40 badges for a club event. Each badge must be at least 5 cm across and have a pin on the back. Every type comes in a standard and a premium version, with these prices per badge:

| diameter | fastening | standard | premium |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 cm | pin | €0.50 | €0.80 |
| 5 cm | magnet | €0.60 | €0.95 |
| 5 cm | pin | €0.75 | €1.10 |
| 6 cm | pin | €0.85 | €1.25 |
| 7 cm | pin | €1.20 | €1.50 |

Mia chooses the cheapest suitable type of badge but decides to buy its premium version.
How much more does she pay than she would for the standard version?
solution: The 4 cm badge is too small and the 5 cm magnet badge has no pin. The cheapest suitable type is the 5 cm badge with a pin: standard €0.75, premium €1.10, so €0.35 more per badge. For 40 badges that is 40 x €0.35 = €14.00. €44.00 is the total premium cost, not the extra.

text:
Sara is painting a bedroom 5 m long, 4 m wide and 2.5 m high. She will paint all four walls and the ceiling, but not the one window, which measures 2 m by 1.5 m. A quarter of the wall area she paints is plaster that needs a second coat. Paint comes in 1-litre tins, and 1 litre covers 10 m².
How many tins must she buy?
solution: Walls: 2 x (5 + 4) x 2.5 = 45 m², minus the 3 m² window = 42 m². Ceiling: 5 x 4 = 20 m². A second coat on a quarter of the walls adds 10.5 m². Total 42 + 20 + 10.5 = 72.5 m², which needs 7.25 litres, so 8 tins. Forgetting the second coat gives 6.2 litres, or 7 tins.

text:
Schools are running after-school cooking clubs in which children prepare meals from fresh vegetables. It is hoped that cooking with vegetables will make children more willing to eat them, and so improve their diets. The clubs should be set up in every school as soon as possible.
Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken this argument?
options: Cooking is not part of the national curriculum.
Some schools do not have a kitchen.
Each club session ends with the children eating a small cake.
Children who attended the clubs enjoyed them but ate no more vegetables at home than other children.
Parents do most of the cooking at home.
solution: The argument rests on the clubs making children eat more vegetables. Evidence that club members eat no more vegetables than others attacks that directly. The curriculum and missing kitchens are practical points that do not show the clubs fail; a small cake does not cancel the effect; parents cooking at home does not show children will refuse vegetables.

text:
A 6-digit door code contains no zeros, and all six digits are different. It is made of two 2-digit numbers, both multiples of 3, followed by their sum, which is also a 2-digit number.
The first digit of the code is 8. What is the last digit?
solution: The first number starts with 8, so it is 81, 84 or 87, and the second must keep the sum below 100. With 81 the partners 12, 15 and 18 all repeat a 1; with 87 the only partner, 12, gives 99. With 84, the partner 12 gives 84 + 12 = 96, and 841296 has six different digits and no zero. So the last digit is 6.

text:
An adult human heart has an average mass of about 300 g, in a body of about 70 kg. The table gives approximate values for some other mammals.

| species | heart mass (g) | body mass (g) |
|---|---|---|
| dog | 120 | 28 000 |
| mouse | 0.15 | 25 |
| rabbit | 6 | 2000 |
| horse | 3600 | 500 000 |
| pig | 290 | 100 000 |

For which species is the ratio of heart mass to body mass closest to that of a human?
solution: Human: 300/70 000, about 0.43%. Dog: 120/28 000, also about 0.43%. Mouse 0.6%, rabbit 0.3%, horse 0.72%, pig 0.29%. Note the units: the human body mass is in kilograms and the table in grams, and the pig's heart mass is close to the human's but its ratio is not.

text:
People read books either to learn something or for enjoyment. Some books, such as textbooks, are full of information, and some people find it easier to learn when information is set out in a book. Other books, such as joke books, contain very little information, so it is unlikely that they are read in order to learn.
Which one of the following conclusions is best supported by the passage above?
options: Textbooks are better books than joke books.
People reading joke books are more likely to be reading for enjoyment than people reading textbooks.
It is easier to learn from a book than from a teacher.
Joke books should not be called books.
solution: If there are only two reasons to read, and joke books are unlikely to be read to learn, then their readers are more likely to be reading for enjoyment than textbook readers are. The passage does not rank the books, compare books with teachers, say textbooks cannot be enjoyed, or question what counts as a book.

text:
Two boats cross a lake between harbours A and B at steady speeds. The fast boat crosses in 30 minutes and the slow boat in 1 hour 30 minutes. Each waits 15 minutes in harbour before setting off back. Both leave harbour A together.
How long has the slow boat been travelling when it meets the fast boat on its way back to A?
solution: Measure position as a fraction of the crossing from A. After t minutes the slow boat is at t/90. The fast boat reaches B at 30 minutes, leaves again at 45 and comes back at 1/30 of the crossing per minute, so it is at 1 - (t - 45)/30. They meet when t/90 = (75 - t)/30, so t = 225/4 = 56.25: about 56 minutes.

text:
Marco notes every visit to the pump in a diary: the odometer reading, the litres bought, and whether he filled up to the brim (✓) or only part of the way.

| date | odometer (km) | litres bought | to the brim? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 May | 10 000 | 20 | |
| 5 May | 10 250 | 30 | ✓ |
| 11 May | 10 600 | 22 | |
| 18 May | 10 900 | 18 | |
| 24 May | 11 250 | 26 | ✓ |
| 29 May | 11 600 | 25 | |

Roughly how many litres does his car use for every 100 km driven?
solution: Only between two visits to the brim do we know exactly how much was used: everything bought after the first, up to and including the second, replaces what was burned. From 10 250 km to 11 250 km (1000 km), 22 + 18 + 26 = 66 litres: 6.6 litres per 100 km. Counting the 30 litres of the first brim-full visit gives 9.6.

text: Which pair of artist and art form is NOT correct?
solution: Sergei Prokofiev was a Russian composer (Peter and the Wolf, Romeo and Juliet), not a painter. Michelangelo sculpted the David, Monet founded Impressionist painting, Vivaldi composed The Four Seasons, and Le Corbusier was a modernist architect.

text: Which of these people did NOT receive the Nobel Peace Prize?
solution: Winston Churchill won a Nobel Prize, but in Literature (1953), for his historical writing and speeches. Mother Teresa (1979), the Dalai Lama (1989), Kofi Annan (2001) and Malala Yousafzai (2014) all received the Peace Prize.

text: In a healthy woman's menstrual cycle, when is the concentration of progesterone in the blood at its highest while LH and FSH are low?
options: in the days just before ovulation
on the first day after menstruation ends
solution: After ovulation the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (and some oestrogen). Progesterone peaks about a week later, in the middle of the luteal phase, and by negative feedback keeps LH and FSH low. LH and FSH peak just before ovulation instead.

text:
These events happen when a person breathes in:
1 The diaphragm contracts and flattens.
2 Air flows into the lungs.
3 The volume of the thorax increases.
4 The pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure.
5 Nerve impulses reach the diaphragm.
Which option lists four of these events in the order in which they happen?
solution: The nerve impulse comes first (5) and makes the diaphragm contract (1). That enlarges the thorax (3), so the pressure inside falls below the air outside (4), and only then does air rush in (2). Of the options, only 5, 1, 3, 4 keeps that order.

text:
Two individuals with the genotype AaBb are crossed. The genes are on different chromosomes.
How many different GENOTYPES are possible among their offspring?
solution: Each gene alone gives three genotypes from Aa x Aa: AA, Aa and aa (and likewise BB, Bb, bb). Independent assortment combines them freely: 3 x 3 = 9. 16 is the number of boxes in the Punnett square, and 4 the number of phenotypes with complete dominance.

text:
Which of the following are made in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?
1 ATP
2 reduced NADP
3 glucose
solution: In the thylakoids, light drives the making of ATP and reduced NADP (and releases oxygen from water). Those two products then power the Calvin cycle in the stroma, which is where carbon dioxide is fixed and sugars such as glucose are made. 1 and 2 only.

text:
A person is heterozygous, Bb, for one gene. Which row shows the alleles present in each kind of cell?

| | cell in G1 of interphase | cell at the end of meiosis I | gamete |
|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | Bb | Bb | B or b |
| row 2 | BBbb | Bb | Bb |
| row 3 | Bb | BB or bb | B or b |
| row 4 | BBbb | BBbb | B or b |
| row 5 | B or b | BB or bb | Bb |
solution: Before DNA replication (G1) the cell has one copy of each homologue: Bb. After replication each chromosome is two identical chromatids, and meiosis I separates the homologues, so each cell gets both chromatids of ONE chromosome: BB or bb. Meiosis II splits the chromatids, so each gamete has a single allele: B or b. Row 3.

text: In a knee joint, in which tissue are chondrocytes found?
solution: Chondrocytes are the cells of cartilage (Greek chondros), which caps the ends of bones in a joint. They sit in small spaces (lacunae) in the matrix they make. Bone has osteocytes, tendons have fibroblasts and muscle has muscle fibres.

text:
A labelled single strand of DNA with the bases TTAGCCGAT is washed over four spots. Each spot carries a short probe, and a probe binds if its bases pair with a stretch of the sample, base for base, in the order written.

| spot | probe |
|---|---|
| 1 | AATCGG |
| 2 | TTAGCC |
| 3 | GGCTA |
| 4 | ATCGAA |

Which spots will bind the sample?
solution: Write the complementary bases of the sample (A with T, C with G): TTAGCCGAT pairs with AATCGGCTA. Probe 1 (AATCGG) matches its first six bases and probe 3 (GGCTA) its last five. Probe 2 repeats the sample's own bases, which cannot pair, and ATCGAA appears nowhere in the complement. 1 and 3 only.

text:
Which row lists events in the order in which they happen in ONE cell cycle, starting from interphase?

| | first | second | third | fourth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | DNA replicates | chromosomes condense | chromatids separate | cytoplasm divides |
| row 2 | chromosomes condense | DNA replicates | chromatids separate | cytoplasm divides |
| row 3 | DNA replicates | chromatids separate | chromosomes condense | cytoplasm divides |
| row 4 | chromosomes condense | nuclear envelope breaks down | DNA replicates | cytoplasm divides |
| row 5 | DNA replicates | cytoplasm divides | chromosomes condense | chromatids separate |
solution: DNA is copied in S phase of interphase. In prophase the chromosomes condense; in anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled apart; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm at the end. Chromatids cannot separate before the chromosomes have condensed, and DNA cannot replicate after condensing in the same cycle.

text: Which one of the following is NOT a protein?
solution: Glycogen is a branched polysaccharide of glucose, the storage carbohydrate of animals. Insulin is a hormone, haemoglobin a transport protein, collagen a structural protein and amylase an enzyme; all are chains of amino acids.

text:
A toxin blocks the voltage-gated potassium channels in an axon membrane but leaves all other channels and pumps working.
Which effect is most likely?
options: The axon could not depolarise at all.
The resting potential would become much more negative.
Repolarisation after an action potential would be slowed.
Sodium ions could no longer enter the axon.
The threshold for an action potential would be lowered.
solution: During an action potential, sodium channels open and the inside becomes positive; voltage-gated potassium channels then open and potassium leaves, bringing the inside back to negative (repolarisation). Block those channels and the membrane stays depolarised longer. Sodium entry, and so depolarisation, still works.

text:
Put these structures from a human liver cell in order of size, smallest first:
1 ribosome
2 lysosome
3 nucleus
solution: A ribosome is about 25 nanometres across, a lysosome about 0.1-1 micrometre, and the nucleus about 5-10 micrometres, the largest structure in most cells. Smallest first: ribosome, lysosome, nucleus.

text:
In a leaf cell of a plant, where can DNA replication take place?
1 the nucleus
2 the mitochondria
3 the chloroplasts
solution: The chromosomes in the nucleus replicate before cell division, but mitochondria and chloroplasts also carry their own small, circular DNA, which they copy when they divide. All three.

text:
Which of the following provide evidence for evolution?
1 the same pattern of limb bones in the arm of a human, the wing of a bat and the flipper of a whale
2 the fossil record
3 similarities between the DNA sequences of different species
solution: Homologous structures (1) show shared ancestry adapted to different uses; fossils (2) show how forms changed over time; and DNA (3) shows species are more similar the more recently they shared an ancestor. All three are standard lines of evidence.

text:
2.2 g of a hydrocarbon contains 1.8 g of carbon.
Which could be its molecular formula?
[Relative atomic masses: H = 1; C = 12]

Ethanoic acid reacts with excess ethanol to form ethyl ethanoate:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH + C_2H_5OH \rightarrow CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O}\)
12.0 g of ethanoic acid gives 11.0 g of ethyl ethanoate.
What is the percentage yield?
[\(M_r\): ethanoic acid = 60; ethyl ethanoate = 88]
solution: 12.0 g of acid is 12.0/60 = 0.200 mol, and the reaction is 1 : 1, so the most ester possible is 0.200 x 88 = 17.6 g. Yield = 11.0/17.6 x 100 = 62.5%. Comparing grams directly (11.0/12.0 = 91.7%) ignores the different molar masses.

text:
At 50 °C, the ionic product of pure water is \(K_w = 5.5 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{mol^2\,L^{-2}}\), larger than its value at 25 °C.
Which of the following statements about pure water at 50 °C is/are correct?
1 It contains equal concentrations of hydrogen and hydroxide ions.
2 Its pH is below 7.
3 It is acidic.
solution: Each water molecule that ionises gives one \(\mathrm{H^+}\) and one \(\mathrm{OH^-}\), so they stay equal (1). \([\mathrm{H^+}] = \sqrt{5.5 \times 10^{-14}} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{-7}\), giving pH about 6.6 (2). But neutral means \([\mathrm{H^+}] = [\mathrm{OH^-}]\), not pH 7, so the water is still neutral (3 wrong).

text: How many unpaired electrons does a phosphorus atom (atomic number 15) have in its ground state?
solution: Phosphorus is \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3\). The three 3p electrons go one into each of the three p orbitals before any pair up (Hund's rule), so all three are unpaired. 5 counts all the outer electrons, including the paired 3s two.

text:
An ionic compound has the formula (mathrm{X_2Y}).
Which pair of atomic numbers could X and Y have?
solution: \(\mathrm{X_2Y}\) needs X to form \(\mathrm{X^+}\) and Y to form \(\mathrm{Y^{2-}}\): X in Group 1, Y in Group 16. 19 is potassium and 8 is oxygen: \(\mathrm{K_2O}\). 12 and 17 give \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\) (\(\mathrm{XY_2}\)), 11 and 17 give NaCl, 13 and 16 give \(\mathrm{Al_2S_3}\), and carbon with oxygen is covalent.

text:
Butan-1-ol and ethoxyethane are isomers, both \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\). Butan-1-ol boils at 118 °C and ethoxyethane at 35 °C.
Which statement explains the difference?
options: Ethoxyethane has the larger relative molecular mass.
Butan-1-ol molecules can hydrogen-bond to each other, but ethoxyethane molecules cannot.
Butan-1-ol has weaker London forces than ethoxyethane.
The covalent bonds in butan-1-ol are stronger, so they take more energy to break on boiling.
solution: Butan-1-ol has an O-H group, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other. In ethoxyethane the oxygen is bonded only to carbon atoms, so the molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other. Isomers have the same molecular mass, and boiling breaks intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.

text:
In a compound, potassium has oxidation number +1, manganese +7 and oxygen -2.
Which formula is correct for this neutral compound?
solution: The oxidation numbers of a neutral compound add up to zero. \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\): +1 + 7 - 8 = 0. Checking the rest: \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\) gives +1, \(\mathrm{KMnO_3}\) +2, \(\mathrm{K(MnO_4)_2}\) -1 and \(\mathrm{K_3MnO_4}\) +2. (In real \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), manganese is +6.)

text: What is the structural formula of methyl propanoate?
solution: An ester is named alcohol part first, acid part second. Methyl propanoate comes from propanoic acid (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}\)) with its H replaced by a methyl group: \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOCH_3}\). The first option is ethyl ethanoate (the same formula, other way round), then butanoic acid, propyl methanoate and pentan-3-one.

text: Butane, (mathrm{C_4H_{10}}), burns completely in excess oxygen. When the equation is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the ratio of oxygen molecules used to carbon dioxide molecules formed?
solution: One butane gives 4 \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and 5 \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), which hold 8 + 5 = 13 oxygen atoms, so 6.5 \(\mathrm{O_2}\). Doubling to whole numbers: \(\mathrm{2C_4H_{10} + 13O_2 \rightarrow 8CO_2 + 10H_2O}\). \(\mathrm{O_2 : CO_2}\) = 13 : 8.

text:
A salt dissolves to 80 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C, but only 30 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. 200 g of water at 60 °C is saturated with the salt and then cooled to 20 °C.
What mass of solid salt crystallises out?
solution: Scale to 200 g of water: it holds 160 g at 60 °C but only 60 g at 20 °C. The difference, 160 - 60 = 100 g, comes out of solution. 50 g is the per-100 g figure, forgetting there are 200 g of water.

text:
Which two of these oxides give ALKALINE solutions with water?
\(\mathrm{Na_2O} \quad \mathrm{SO_3} \quad \mathrm{CaO} \quad \mathrm{CO}\)
solution: Metal oxides are basic: sodium oxide gives sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide gives calcium hydroxide. Non-metal oxides tend to be acidic: \(\mathrm{SO_3}\) gives sulfuric acid. Carbon monoxide is a neutral oxide and does not react with water at all.

text: Which one of these 0.01 mol/L aqueous solutions has a pH below 7?
solution: Ammonium nitrate is the salt of a weak base and a strong acid; \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\) donates a proton to water, so the solution is acidic. KCl (strong acid, strong base) is neutral; sodium carbonate and sodium ethanoate are salts of weak acids and are alkaline, and NaOH is a strong base.

subject: Mathematics
text: If \(\log_{10} y = 3\log_{10} x + 2\), which expression gives \(y\)?
solution: \(3\log_{10} x = \log_{10} x^3\) and \(2 = \log_{10} 100\), so \(\log_{10} y = \log_{10} x^3 + \log_{10} 100 = \log_{10}(100x^3)\), giving \(y = 100x^3\). Adding logs multiplies the numbers; it does not add them.

subject: Physics
text:
Which equation has consistent units on both sides?
[s = distance; u, v = velocities; a = acceleration; t = time; m = mass; F = force; P = power; W = work]
solution: Force x velocity is N x m/s = J/s = W, and work / time is also J/s, so both terms on the right are power, matching P. In the others: \(at^2\) is a distance, not a velocity; \(at\) is a velocity, not a distance; \(mv\) is momentum, not force; \(P/t\) is W/s, not J.

subject: Mathematics
text:
\(3x + 2y = 16\) and \(x - y = 2\).
What is the value of \(xy\)?
solution: From the second equation \(x = y + 2\). Substituting: \(3(y + 2) + 2y = 16\), so \(5y = 10\), \(y = 2\) and \(x = 4\). Then \(xy = 8\). Check: \(12 + 4 = 16\) and \(4 - 2 = 2\).

subject: Mathematics
text:
The mean of four numbers \(p\), \(q\), \(r\) and \(s\) is 5.
What is the mean of the five numbers \(p - 1\), \(q + 3\), \(r + 2\), \(s\) and 6?
solution: Work with totals: \(p + q + r + s = 4 \times 5 = 20\). The new five numbers add up to \(20 - 1 + 3 + 2 + 0 + 6 = 30\). Their mean is 30/5 = 6; 30 is the total, and dividing by 4 instead of 5 gives 7.5.

subject: Mathematics
text: Evaluate \((53^2 - 47^2) - (21^2 - 19^2)\) without a calculator.
solution: Use \(a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)\). \(53^2 - 47^2 = 6 \times 100 = 600\) and \(21^2 - 19^2 = 2 \times 40 = 80\). The difference is 600 - 80 = 520; adding instead of subtracting gives 680.

subject: Physics
text:
A 0.50 kg copper block cools from 80 °C to 30 °C and gives out 9750 J of heat.
Which expression gives c for copper from these figures?
solution: \(Q = mc\Delta T\), so \(c = \dfrac{Q}{m\Delta T}\). The temperature change is 80 - 30 = 50 K (a change of 50 °C is a change of 50 K), not the final 30 °C. That gives \(9750/(0.50 \times 50) = 390\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), close to copper's real value.
